{\large\bfseries Do LLM Judges Agree on the Quality of Explanations? A Two-Panel
Reliability Study\par}

\medskip

\section*{Abstract}
Large language models (LLMs) are used as judges of the quality of explanations because
they cost less than human raters. That use assumes that different judges give the same
explanation the same score. This study measures that agreement. Three LLM judges scored
192 post-hoc explanations (SHAP, LIME, Anchors, DiCE; three tabular
datasets) on seven dimensions with a 1--5 rubric, in two panels of different models. The
second panel also varied the prompt, repeated every call three times and scored the cases
again without the technical metrics
(5,760 calls). Agreement was measured with the intraclass
correlation ICC(1,1). Over all cases no dimension reached 0.75 in either panel (highest
values 0.601 and 0.731). That
coefficient overstates agreement on the explanations: up to
67\% of the variance of the scores lay between explanation
methods. Among the SHAP cases no dimension exceeded
0.19, with or without the metrics; among the LIME cases five
dimensions stayed above 0.6. The mean of the three judges was reliable for separating
methods, not explanations. With the metrics in the prompt the overall score followed
fidelity within every method, and one judge named a metric in
80\% of its answers. Without them that judge
scored higher, the correlation vanished for SHAP and DiCE, and agreement on audit
usefulness fell from 0.66 to
0.42. A single LLM judge of this class should
not be used as a confirmatory measure. Studies using them should report
agreement within method, the number of calls and what the prompt contained.

\noindent\textbf{Keywords:} explainable artificial intelligence; LLM-as-a-judge;
inter-rater reliability; explanation evaluation; intraclass correlation.

\section*{Resumen}
Los modelos de lenguaje de gran tama\~no (LLM) se usan como jueces de la calidad de las
explicaciones por su menor costo. Ese uso supone que jueces
distintos punt\'uan igual la misma explicaci\'on. Este estudio mide esa concordancia. Tres
jueces LLM puntuaron 192 explicaciones post hoc (SHAP, LIME, Anchors,
DiCE; tres conjuntos de datos tabulares) en siete dimensiones con una r\'ubrica de 1 a 5,
en dos paneles. El segundo vari\'o el \emph{prompt}, repiti\'o
cada llamada tres veces y puntu\'o los casos de nuevo sin las m\'etricas t\'ecnicas
(5,760 llamadas). La concordancia se midi\'o con la correlaci\'on
intraclase ICC(1,1). Con todos los casos, ninguna dimensi\'on alcanz\'o 0.75 en ning\'un
panel (m\'aximos: 0.601 y 0.731). Pero hasta el
67\% de la varianza estaba entre m\'etodos.
En los casos de SHAP ninguna dimensi\'on super\'o 0.19, con o
sin m\'etricas; en los de LIME, cinco dimensiones superaron 0.6. La media de los tres
jueces fue fiable para separar m\'etodos, no explicaciones. Con las m\'etricas en el
\emph{prompt}, la puntuaci\'on global sigui\'o la fidelidad en cada m\'etodo, y un juez
nombr\'o una m\'etrica en el 80\% de sus
respuestas. Sin ellas ese juez puntu\'o m\'as alto, la correlaci\'on desapareci\'o para
SHAP y DiCE, y la concordancia en utilidad para auditor\'ia baj\'o de
0.66 a
0.42. Un solo juez LLM de esta clase no deber\'ia
usarse como medida confirmatoria. Los estudios que los usen deber\'ian informar la
concordancia por m\'etodo, el n\'umero de llamadas y el contenido del \emph{prompt}.

\noindent\textbf{Palabras clave:} inteligencia artificial explicable; LLM como juez;
fiabilidad entre evaluadores; evaluaci\'on de explicaciones; correlaci\'on intraclase.

\section{Introduction}

Post-hoc explainers such as SHAP \cite{lundberg2017unified}, LIME \cite{ribeiro2016why},
Anchors \cite{ribeiro2018anchors} and DiCE \cite{mothilal2020dice} are evaluated mostly
with technical proxy metrics: whether the features an explanation ranks first are those
that move the prediction \cite{bhatt2020evaluating}, and whether similar inputs receive
similar explanations \cite{alvarezmelis2018robustness}. These metrics are cheap and
repeatable, but they do not say whether an explanation is clear, plausible or useful to
the person who reads it \cite{doshivelez2017rigorous,jacovi2020faithfulness}. Studies with
people measure that, at a cost that limits their size, and their results do not always
agree with the proxies \cite{bucinca2020proxy,bansal2021whole}.

Large language models (LLMs) used as judges promise a third source of evidence: scores of
meaning at the scale of a proxy metric. In other fields LLM judges show position and
verbosity biases and can agree with each other without being right
\cite{zheng2023judging,gu2024llmjudge}, and their agreement with people depends on the
task \cite{wu2025userperceptions,zhou2025medthink}. Reviews of the evaluation of
explanations organise proxy metrics, benchmarks, expert judgments and user studies
\cite{nauta2023anecdotal,mohseni2021survey,longo2024manifesto}; LLM judges are the newest
source and the least validated. In a scoping corpus of 44 papers
on the evaluation of post-hoc explanations assembled for this work, only
4 concern LLM judges, one of them a survey.

A judge can stand in for a human rater only if it is first reliable, that is, if another
judge of the same kind gives the same explanation the same score. Reliability is the
weaker requirement and comes before validity: a score that changes with the judge cannot
be valid for a property of the explanation. This paper measures it. Three LLM judges
scored 192 explanations on seven dimensions, in two panels of different
models. Four questions are answered:

\begin{enumerate}
\item Do three LLM judges agree on the score of an explanation, on each dimension?
\item Is their agreement about the explanation, or about the method that produced it?
\item How much do the scores depend on the rubric wording, on repetition and on how they
are aggregated?
\item Do the scores follow the technical metrics of the explanation, and what remains
when the judges are not shown them?
\end{enumerate}

\section{Materials and methods}

\subsection{Cases}

The cases are 192 single explanations, each of one prediction of a
binary classifier, from 174 distinct instances. They
were drawn from the stored runs of a public benchmark \cite{herrera2026framework}:
96 from Adult \cite{becker1996adult},
53 from German Credit \cite{hofmann1994statlog}
and 43 from Breast Cancer Wisconsin
\cite{wolberg1993breast}. They cover 4 model families
(logistic regression, random forest, XGBoost and a multilayer perceptron) and four
explainers: 76 Anchors,
52 SHAP, 32 LIME and
32 DiCE explanations. LIME and DiCE cases come from
Adult only. Sampling was stratified by the outcome of the prediction
(52 true positives, 47 true
negatives, 46 false positives and
47 false negatives).

Each case is a record with the dataset, the model family, the explainer, the prediction,
the outcome of the prediction (TP, TN, FP or FN), the explanation as text and the
technical metrics computed for that explanation in the benchmark: fidelity, stability,
sparsity, faithfulness gap and runtime. The benchmark renders every explanation with one
template, a list of ten features with a weight. For SHAP and LIME the list holds the
attributions the method produced, for example ``worst area: $-$0.1336; worst perimeter:
$-$0.0935; \ldots''. For Anchors and DiCE it does not hold the explanation in its own
form: an anchor rule appears as weights of one for the features of the rule and zero for
the others, without thresholds (``education-num: 1.0000; capital-gain: 1.0000; age:
0.0000; \ldots''), and a counterfactual appears as the size of the change of each
feature, without direction, new value or new outcome (``age: 1.6182; fnlwgt: 0.0000;
\ldots''). The median number of zero-weight items is
7 of ten for Anchors and
8 for DiCE. The
84 SHAP and LIME cases are therefore the main analysis; the
108 Anchors and DiCE cases are reported beside them as
scores of that rendering.

\subsection{Judges, rubric and conditions}

A judge received the rubric and one case record, and returned an integer from 1 to 5 and
a short rationale for each of seven dimensions: clarity, concision, actionability, audit
usefulness, completeness, semantic plausibility and overall quality. The rubric gives a
one-sentence definition of each dimension and anchors for the scores 1, 3 and 5.

The first panel was GPT-4o mini (OpenAI), Claude 3 Haiku (Anthropic) and Gemini 1.5
Flash (Google), with temperature 0. Its prompt templates and raw responses were not
kept; its aggregate tables were, and they are the source of its values here. The study
was therefore run again on the same cases with a second panel, GPT-5.4 mini, Claude Haiku
4.5 and Gemini 3.8 Flash, also with temperature 0, with templates rebuilt from the
recorded rubric. The second run is a second measurement, not a reproduction: besides the
models, the two runs differ in the templates, in the output limit and in the cases with
scores from the three judges (147 against all
192), and the prompt condition and aggregation behind the tables of the
first are not recorded.

The second panel scored every case under four prompt conditions:

\begin{itemize}
\item \emph{Primary}: the rubric above; the true-label field of the record is empty.
Three calls per case and judge.
\item \emph{Label stated}: the same rubric; the true label is given. Three calls.
\item \emph{Alternative rubric}: the same seven dimensions with every definition
reworded, anchors at all five scale points and the dimensions in another order; the true
label is given. Three calls.
\item \emph{Clean}: the rubric of the primary condition word for word; the record has no
technical metrics, no outcome of the prediction and no true label. One call.
\end{itemize}

The first three conditions have a defect that was found after they were run: the record
contains the outcome of the prediction, which together with the prediction gives the true
label, and it contains the technical metrics. In those conditions the judges therefore
scored an explanation with its label and its metrics in view. The clean condition was
added to remove both. Of the 5,760 calls,
5,756 returned valid scores.

\subsection{Statistical analysis}

Agreement among the three judges was measured per dimension with the intraclass
correlation ICC(1,1), the one-way random-effects coefficient for a single rater
\cite{shrout1979intraclass}, with its exact 95\% confidence interval from the $F$
distribution. A dimension is said to have good reliability when the coefficient is 0.75
or more \cite{koo2016guideline}. Krippendorff's alpha for ordinal data
\cite{krippendorff2004reliability} was computed as a check and differed from the ICC by at
most 0.04 in the first panel and
0.001 in the second; it is not tabulated. For the first
panel the ICC uses the 147 cases with three scores.

For the second panel the coefficient of the primary condition is given in three forms:
with the three calls of a judge averaged per case, as in the first analysis of these data;
for one call; and as ICC(1,$k$), the reliability of the mean of the three judges. Two-way
coefficients, ICC(2,1) for absolute agreement and ICC(3,1) for consistency, are reported
as a check of the model, and the share of pairs of judges with the same score as a
description. To separate agreement on the explanation from agreement on the method, the
share of the variance of the case-level mean score that lies between explainers was
computed, and the ICC was computed inside each explainer.

Three sensitivity views are reported for the second panel: the label-stated condition,
the alternative rubric, and a pooled view in which the nine scores of a judge for a case
are averaged. Test-retest agreement is the share of case-and-judge pairs with the same
score in the three calls. The effect of a prompt change is the mean difference in score,
paired by case.

The relation between scores and technical metrics was analysed within each explainer with
Spearman correlations between the overall-quality score, averaged over judges, and
fidelity, stability, sparsity, faithfulness gap and runtime, with Holm's correction
\cite{holm1979simple}. The share of responses whose rationales name a metric was counted
per judge. All analyses other than the ICC of the primary condition were planned after
the first three conditions had been run; each was written down with its date before it
was computed, and the clean condition was specified before it was run.

\section{Results}

\subsection{Agreement over all cases}

Table~\ref{tab:icc} gives the agreement per dimension over all cases. In the first panel
the highest ICC was 0.601 (semantic plausibility); in the second
it was 0.731 (completeness). No dimension reached 0.75 in
either. In the second panel the upper confidence bounds of
two dimensions, completeness and audit
usefulness, were above 0.75. The order of the dimensions differed between the two runs:
audit usefulness rose from 0.376 to
0.699, and clarity and actionability fell to
about zero. Given the differences between the runs listed above, this cannot be
attributed to the judges alone.

The form of the estimate matters. With one call per judge, which is how a judge is
normally used, the coefficients of the five dimensions with some agreement were lower
(completeness 0.675). The mean of the three judges was more
reliable: its ICC(1,$k$) was 0.75 or more on
four dimensions. The two-way coefficients did not
change the reading for absolute agreement (completeness
0.733); for consistency, which ignores a constant
difference between judges, completeness was
0.750 and concision
0.596.

The scores used a narrow part of the scale. For overall quality,
59\% of the scores were
2, and two judges gave the same score in
71\% of the cases and scores within one
point in 99\%. For actionability
86\% of the scores were 1, so the judges
almost always agreed and the coefficient, which needs differences between cases, is near
zero. For clarity one judge hardly varied its score (standard deviation
0.38) and scored on average
0.64 points below the other two.

\subsection{Agreement on the explanation or on the method}

Most of the variation that the judges agreed on was variation between explainers
(Table~\ref{tab:within}). The share of the variance of the case-level mean score that
lay between explainers was 67\% for
completeness, 64\% for overall quality
and 63\% for audit usefulness. Inside
an explainer the picture changes (Figure~\ref{fig:icc}). Among the
52 SHAP cases no dimension exceeded
0.19, and the coefficient of overall quality was
$-$0.19: the three judges did not agree on which
SHAP explanation was better. Among the 32 LIME cases
agreement stayed between 0.63 and
0.75 on five dimensions. Taking SHAP and LIME
together gave 0.73 for completeness, again
because the judges separated the two methods. For Anchors and DiCE, as rendered, the
highest coefficient was 0.46.

\subsection{Rubric wording, aggregation and repetition}

Table~\ref{tab:views} gives the ICC of the second panel, over all cases, under the three
sensitivity views. The alternative rubric moved agreement in both directions: concision
rose from 0.360 to 0.650,
clarity fell from 0.026 to
$-$0.249, and completeness reached
0.753. It moved the scores by up to
0.50 points (median over judges and dimensions
0.12). In the pooled view
two dimensions exceeded 0.75, completeness
(0.839) and audit usefulness
(0.820): averaging nine scores removes the
variation between repeated calls and raises the coefficient.

Repeated calls with temperature 0 did not always return the same score. Over the seven
dimensions, Claude Haiku 4.5 gave the same score in its three calls in
93\% to 99\% of the
cases, Gemini 3.8 Flash in 65\% to
91\% and GPT-5.4 mini in
33\% to 87\%.

Stating the label changed the scores by 0.14 points at
most. Since the primary condition already allowed the label to be derived, that
comparison is not a test. A direct one is available: in the primary condition the mean
overall-quality score was 2.32 for cases with a correct
prediction and 2.29 for cases with a wrong one (Mann-Whitney
$p =$ 0.695). The judges could know whether the model was right,
and it did not move the score.

\subsection{Scores and the technical metrics}

With the metrics printed in the prompt, the overall-quality score followed them
(Table~\ref{tab:metrics}). It rose with fidelity inside the four explainers (Spearman
correlation from 0.35 to
0.59), in all four after Holm's
correction. Of the other 16 correlations two remained after the correction: stability for
Anchors and sparsity for LIME, the latter on few distinct values.

The rationales show the same thing directly, and show that the judges differed. A metric

\subsection{The clean condition}

In the clean condition the judges saw the explanation without its metrics, the outcome of
the prediction or the label; all 576 calls returned valid scores.
Table~\ref{tab:clean} compares it with one call of the primary condition. Three things
changed and one did not.

First, the judge that had named the metrics most often scored differently without them.
The mean score of Claude Haiku 4.5 rose on every dimension, by
0.30 points for overall quality and
0.52 for audit usefulness; the mean
overall-quality scores of the other two judges moved by
0.01 and
0.01.

Second, the relation with fidelity was no longer general. With one call of the primary
condition the correlation between the overall-quality score and fidelity was
0.48 for SHAP, 0.56
for DiCE, 0.48 for LIME and
0.26 for Anchors. In the clean condition it was
$-$0.05 for SHAP and 0.08 for
DiCE, and 0.41 for LIME and
0.26 for Anchors, neither of which remained after
Holm's correction over the four tests. For SHAP and DiCE the score had followed the
printed number; for LIME and Anchors something visible in the rendered explanation goes
with fidelity.

Third, agreement over all cases fell where the metrics had fed it most: audit usefulness
from 0.66 to
0.42, completeness from
0.68 to 0.58
and overall quality from 0.63 to
0.57. Semantic plausibility and concision did not
change.

What did not change is the pattern inside the explainers. Among the SHAP cases no
dimension exceeded 0.20 in the clean condition, and among
the LIME cases agreement on completeness, semantic plausibility and overall quality
stayed between 0.63 and
0.69. The absence of agreement on SHAP
explanations is therefore not produced by the metrics in the prompt, and the agreement on
LIME explanations is not either.

\section{Discussion}

The first question has a negative answer in both panels: over all cases no dimension
reached good agreement. The second question changes what that answer means. A coefficient
of about 0.7 over all cases suggests judges that are close to usable. Most of it was
agreement that SHAP records deserve higher scores than Anchors or DiCE records. Inside
SHAP, where a user would want a judge to tell a better explanation from a worse one,
the agreement of three judges was near zero, with or without the metrics in the prompt. LIME is the
exception, and it is not explained by the metrics; its cases come from one dataset, and
why its explanations draw agreement is not established here. A study that reports one agreement coefficient over
explanations of several methods is reporting, in large part, that its judges can tell the
methods apart.

The same decomposition limits what the mean of a panel offers. The mean of the three
judges was reliable over all cases, so a panel can rank methods consistently. It was not
shown to rank explanations of one method, and whether its ranking of methods is right is
a question of validity that these data cannot answer.

The third question has a practical answer. Rewording the rubric moved the ICC of
concision by about 0.3 and that of clarity in the opposite direction. Averaging repeated
calls and prompt variants before computing the coefficient raised two dimensions above
the threshold, because the average hides the variation of a judge with itself, and that
variation is not small: with temperature 0 one judge repeated its score almost always and
another in fewer than half of the cases on some dimensions.

The fourth question shows that what is put in the prompt becomes part of what is
measured. One judge used the printed metrics heavily, said so in its rationales and
scored higher without them; the other two hardly changed. For SHAP and DiCE the relation
between score and fidelity existed only while fidelity was printed. A judge that is given
technical metrics may return them in another form, and then its score adds no independent
evidence about meaning.

The study has limits. It measures agreement among LLM judges and has no human scores, so
it says nothing about whether the judges are right. Both panels are small, low-cost
models, and the conclusions are limited to that class. The templates and responses of
the first panel were lost, so its condition and aggregation are unknown, the second run
is not a reproduction, and the decomposition by explainer cannot be made for it. Anchors
and DiCE were scored in a rendering that is not their own; their scores, the floor of
actionability and part of the variance between explainers may come from it. The cases
are unbalanced across explainers and datasets, and the groups inside an explainer are
small. The clean condition has one call per judge. Except for the ICC of the primary
condition, the analyses were planned after the first responses existed.

\section{Conclusions}

Three small LLM judges did not reach good agreement on any of seven dimensions of
explanation quality, in two panels (highest ICC(1,1) 0.601 and
0.731). What agreement there was concerned mainly the method:
up to 67\% of the variance of the scores lay between
explainers, and among SHAP explanations agreement was near zero on every dimension, with
or without technical metrics in the prompt. The mean of three judges was reliable for
comparing methods and unverified for comparing explanations. Scores changed with the
rubric wording, with repetition and with the content of the prompt, where one judge
largely restated the metrics it was shown. A single LLM judge of this class should not be
used as a confirmatory measure of the quality of an explanation. Studies that use LLM
judges should report agreement within each method, the number of calls per item, the
aggregation rule and what the prompt contained. The comparison with human raters and the
scoring of rules and counterfactuals in their own form are the next steps.
